A simple pattern: "For [customer] who [problem], we [what you do] so you can [result]." For example: "For busy pet owners who work late, we walk your dog at lunch so it gets exercise and you do not rush home." A clear offer is specific, honest and easy to repeat. It avoids vague phrases like "best quality" that do not say what the customer gets.
prompt: A founder wrote a clear offer but has no idea if customers care about the stated result. What should she check?
choices: A. Whether target customers say that result matters to them | B. Whether her family likes the wording | C. Whether the sentence has a nice rhythm when read aloud | D. Whether the font matches her logo
correct_answer: Whether target customers say that result matters to them
feedback: The offer's promised result must matter to the actual customers.
wrong_choices: B: family is not the target customer | C: style is secondary | D: not relevant to customer interest

outcome_title: Apply a documented early decision (solving a problem you have and checking that others share it) to a new business
intro: Your own problem is a clue, not proof. If you are frustrated by something, ask: do many other people have this same frustration, and do they spend money on it? One person is a sample of one. A market is many people with the same need who will pay. You find out by asking others about their experience and by testing whether they will buy, not by assuming they feel what you feel.
prompt: Your own frustration with a product is best described as what?
choices: A. A clue worth checking | B. A guarantee of sales | C. Proof of a large market | D. A finished business plan
correct_answer: A clue worth checking
feedback: Your own problem is a starting clue.
wrong_choices: B: nothing guarantees sales | C: one person is not a market | D: it is only a start

set_title: Founder case: Spanx and a problem the founder had
section_skill: Apply it: from a personal problem to a tested idea
outcome_title: Apply a documented early decision (solving a problem you have and checking that others share it) to a new business
intro: Documented history: Sara Blakely cut the feet off control-top pantyhose to wear under white pants. She started Spanx in 2000 with $5,000 of her own savings. Several hosiery manufacturers turned her down before one agreed to make the product, and she got it into the Neiman Marcus department store. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation, not her words): a problem you have yourself can be a starting point, but you still need evidence that many others share it and will buy. One success story does not guarantee the same result.
prompt: Ana hates that her reusable water bottle leaks in her bag. Which first step best applies the lesson?
choices: A. Post a logo and wait for orders | B. Ask only her mother whether bottles leak | C. Buy a bottle factory before telling anyone about the idea | D. Survey commuters about leaking bottles and what they do now
correct_answer: Survey commuters about leaking bottles and what they do now
feedback: Asking many commuters checks whether her problem is shared.
wrong_choices: A: no evidence gathered | B: one person is not enough | C: too much spending first
